slides.title: Chapter 5: Wallet Recovery
slides.say: Chapter 4 made one key; chapter 5 makes ALL of them recoverable from twelve words you can write on paper - and shows what happens to people who skip the writing. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5.
slides.concept: One seed, twelve words, and every key you will ever need back

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Five parts, ending at a tested backup. One story costs 7,002 BTC, one finds 200,000, and one explains the twelve words in your pocket. A question to think about is this: which part do you expect to be hardest? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in every section.
slides.concept: Five parts - and at the end, a backup you have actually tested

slides.title: Keys in wallets
slides.say: This first branch of the chapter asks what a Bitcoin wallet really contains and where its keys come from. The chapter begins by correcting a common belief. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in Wallet keys.
slides.concept: From a bag of keys to one recoverable seed

slides.title: Two guesses from 7,002 bitcoin
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 2021-01-12. In 2011 Stefan Thomas was paid 7,002 BTC for making an animated explainer about bitcoin. He put the keys on an encrypted IronKey drive, wrote the password on a paper he later lost, and the drive allows ten guesses before locking forever. The source is the New York Times, 2021-01-12, 'Lost Passwords Lock Millionaires Out of Their Bitcoin Fortunes': 7,002 BTC, ten guesses, eight used.
slides.concept: Memory is not a backup - this chapter is the alternative

slides.title: From loose keys to one seed
slides.say: Independent key generation is the method in which a wallet application creates each of the keys that it plans to use independently of the others. Each is a fresh random number with no connection to the rest, and the wallet database is simply the collection of them. A question to think about is this: what breaks if a deterministic wallet's RNG is biased? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in Independent key generation and Deterministic key generation.
slides.concept: Back up one secret once, instead of every key forever

slides.title: Recovery codes
slides.say: A recovery code is the short, written form of a wallet's seed: a sequence of words, or in one case a string of letters and digits, from which every key of a deterministic wallet can be computed again. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in Recovery codes.
slides.concept: Entropy, dressed for handwriting

slides.title: Twelve words between you and 128 bits
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 2013-09-10. The team building the first hardware signing device faced a human problem: nobody transcribes 128 raw bits correctly. Their 2013 proposal, BIP 39, encodes entropy as ordinary words from a curated list of 2,048 - eleven bits a word, a checksum folded in, a key-stretching function from words to seed. The source is BIP 39, 'Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys', authors Palatinus, Rusnak, Voisine, Bowe, dated 2013-09-10, in bitcoin/bips.
slides.concept: The recovery code is an interface between humans and entropy

slides.title: Words to bits, measured
slides.say: The length of a recovery code is not a free choice: it is determined by the amount of entropy. The chapter prints the relation as a table with four columns, entropy in bits, checksum in bits, entropy plus checksum, and recovery code words, whose five rows run from 128 bits and 12 words to 256 bits and 24 words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: why eleven bits a word? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in Code length and Word list.
slides.concept: Eleven bits a word; the checksum rides along

slides.title: From words to seed, slowly on purpose
slides.say: PBKDF2 is the second password-based key derivation function of the PKCS #5 standard, and it is the particular key-stretching function BIP39 names. Its specification defines it as applying a pseudorandom function to derive keys, with four inputs: a password, a salt, an iteration count and the intended length of the derived key in octets, and says it is recommended for new applications (Moriarty et al., 2017). A question to think about is this: where must the passphrase NOT be stored? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in PBKDF2 and Recovery code passphrase.
slides.concept: The passphrase changes everything - by design

slides.title: The tree and its paths
slides.say: A hierarchical deterministic wallet, which the chapter and the standards abbreviate to HD wallet, is a wallet whose keys form a tree, every node of which is computed from the seed. The book's glossary calls the hierarchical deterministic protocol the key creation and transfer protocol of BIP32, which allows creating child keys from parent keys in a hierarchy, and an HD wallet a wallet using that protocol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in Hierarchical deterministic wallet.
slides.concept: One seed, a numbered key for every purpose

slides.title: One seed, a tree of keys
slides.say: Hierarchical deterministic key generation, usually shortened to HD, is the standard way to derive keys from a seed. It is defined in BIP32, a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal by Pieter Wuille that has the status Deployed (Wuille, 2012). A question to think about is this: why carry a chain code at all? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in Hierarchical deterministic key generation and Child key derivation.
slides.concept: Two 32-byte halves at every node keep the tree alive

slides.title: Hardened or not: one question, two columns
slides.say: Hardened derivation is the alternative derivation function that breaks the relationship between the parent public key and the child chain code. Think about this case: read m/84h/0h/0h/0/2: which hops could a watch-only server have taken itself? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in Hardened child key derivation and Private child key derivation.
slides.concept: The h in a path is a security decision, not decoration

slides.title: The paths everyone agreed on
slides.say: BIP44 is the layout that gives a tree its familiar shape. The chapter says that, extending BIP43, BIP44 proposes a multi-account structure as purpose number 44 with a prime, that all wallets following the structure are identified by using only the branch m/44', and that the structure consists of five predefined tree levels: purpose, coin type, account, change and address index (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Think about this case: your phone wallet says 'account 0'. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in BIP44 structure and BIP84 path for native segwit.
slides.concept: m/84h/0h/0h/0/0 - and Core derives the same address

slides.title: Beyond keys
slides.say: This branch is about everything in a wallet that a seed cannot reproduce. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in Backing up data that is not keys.
slides.concept: What else must survive, and how wallets ship

slides.title: Watch-only: the shop holds no keys
slides.say: Deploying an extended public key means installing the public half of a branch on a machine that needs to receive but not to spend. Think about this case: a donation page went viral and used 400 addresses. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in Extended public key deployment and Gap limit.
slides.concept: Publish the xpub; the keys never feel the internet

slides.title: The 200,000 BTC in a forgotten wallet file
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 2014-03-21. Chapter 1 told how Mt. Gox collapsed owing 850,000 BTC. Three weeks after the bankruptcy filing came a twist: the company reported finding about 200,000 BTC in an old-format wallet file that had sat unused since 2011. The source is Mt. Gox announcement of 2014-03-20/21 reporting approximately 200,000 BTC found in an old-format wallet; summarized with the bankruptcy chronology at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Gox.
slides.concept: Backups do not expire - treat old wallet files as live keys

slides.title: Split the secret, not the risk
slides.say: Secret sharing is a way of splitting one secret into several parts with a threshold. SLIP39's description is the clearest: the scheme splits a secret into a number of unique parts, of which any threshold-many are required to reconstruct it, and knowledge of fewer than the required number does not leak information about the secret (Rusnak et al., 2017). A question to think about is this: where do five shares live so no burglary, flood, or sibling feud collects three? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in Secret sharing and SLIP39 share set.
slides.concept: Three of five recovers; two of five learns nothing

slides.title: Test the backup, not your luck
slides.say: Testing a backup means performing the recovery while it is still optional. It is the action the chapter's last sentence asks for: it is up to the reader to actually use the systems available to make good backups and regularly test them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: when did you last restore a backup of anything? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in Testing a backup and Data loss.
slides.concept: A backup counts only after a successful restore drill

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.say: Five lines, one per part; the agenda names the slides that prove each. A question to think about is this: which line would you defend first, and with which slide? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in every section.
slides.concept: If a line feels unproven, its part's slides carry the receipt

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.say: Everything here is free. Homework: generate a THROWAWAY twelve-word code, restore it in a second wallet, and bring the one surprise you hit to class. A question to think about is this: which of the four closing chips does your current phone wallet fail? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 5, in Deploying keys in practice.
slides.concept: Twelve words on paper beat every password you have ever memorized
